title: True or false? – Charity and social justice

instruction.text: You will hear a report from Shortcut News Radio on charity and social justice. Linda Thompson visited a food bank and talked to volunteers, people seeking help, and experts. Listen to the report and decide which of the statements are true and which are false. Tick the correct boxes.

atoms.sound: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>It’s a grey afternoon in East London, and the queue outside the Bridgeway Community Trust Foodbank is already stretching past the corner shop. Volunteers carry crates of tins and fresh vegetables through a narrow doorway. A hand-written sign says: ‘No judgement. Take what you need.’</voice> <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>Inside, the mood is calm, almost routine. But the numbers behind this routine are anything but normal. Across London, one major network of food banks has more than doubled the number of emergency food parcels over the last five years—from just over 200,000 in 2019/20 to around 455,000 recently. That’s roughly over a thousand parcels a day—and it doesn’t even include every independent food bank or community kitchen. However, it is becoming increasingly difficult to meet the increased demand, says Madeleine Powell from the Bridgeway food bank's management team.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10_chirp'>Some people come with a referral, others just walk in because they’ve run out of options. But slowly but surely, we are running out of resources. And I don't mean volunteers. Sure, we used to see spikes around Christmas. Nevertheless, we can always rely on a constant number of helpers. The only problem is: Donations aren’t keeping up. Supermarkets waste less than they used to, which is good—but it means we have less to give. At the same time, we feel that the situation is becoming more serious by the day, that more and more people are coming to us – and we simply cannot cope with this.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>Bridgeway doesn’t call itself a ‘charity shop for the poor.’ They call it ‘community support.’ Members can also use a small pantry scheme: a few pounds for a basket of basics. It’s meant to feel more like shopping than begging. Near the tea station, I meet Daniel, a delivery driver who lost hours when his company cut shifts.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m5_chirp'>You know … I work. That’s the mad part. But rent went up, energy bills went up, and food just… exploded in price. I skipped meals so my daughter wouldn’t. Coming here was embarrassing at first. Then you realise—this isn’t about being lazy. It’s about the system not adding up.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>That word—system—comes up again and again. Social organisations say food banks are a symptom, not a solution.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m12_chirp'>When families rely on emergency food, it’s not simply individual misfortune. It’s a social justice issue: wages, housing costs, and the safety net. Charity is powerful—it builds solidarity. But it shouldn’t replace rights. Long-term, we need ‘cash-first’ support, so people can choose their food with dignity, rather than depend on whatever is available.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>That’s Tom O’Sullivan, a community organiser and spokesperson for a London social welfare association, working with food banks across the city. For him, the food crisis, as he calls it, is primarily a political failure – especially since there are solutions to all these problems. O’Sullivan again:</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m12_chirp'>And the thing is, charity isn’t the opposite of politics—it’s often the result of politics. People step in when systems fail. But we shouldn’t normalise emergency help as the new safety net. If we’re serious about social justice, we need higher incomes, affordable housing, and crisis support that comes as cash, quickly, so families can make choices—like anyone else.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>Back at Bridgeway, they don’t have time to wait for politicians to finally take action.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f10_chirp'>Look, we can talk policy all day—and I agree, people need proper support, not just parcels. But if someone turns up hungry today, you don’t send them away with a debate. You give them food, you listen, and you help them figure out the next step.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f3_chirp'>So volunteers carry on: they pack bags with pasta, rice, fruit, and baby formula. One volunteer tells me they’re proud of the community spirit—yet worried that society is getting used to crisis as normal. Charity can look like kindness. But in London today, it also looks like an emergency response that refuses to become invisible.</voice>
